00. Overview & the ABCS Framework

Goal: provide a cognitive approach to the osteopathic care of a patient with cardiovascular system disorders, using the ABCS framework:

  • Autonomics — sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation to the heart, and Chapman's points for the cardiovascular/renal systems
  • Biomechanics — related myofascial and skeletal structures, and how restriction can affect the system
  • Circulation — related arteries, veins, and lymphatics; ideal circulation is vital to system function
  • Screening — additional areas to screen for this system
"The Rule of the Artery is Supreme." — A.T. Still
Tissues and organs need oxygen to survive and thrive, and arteries are how they get it.
Required reading: MCOM OCS III & IV OMM Manual, Chapter 3.

01. Autonomics: Sympathetic Innervation to the Heart

  • Sympathetics to the heart arise from T1–T5
  • Preganglionic fibers enter the sympathetic chain via the white rami communicantes, then either:
    1. Synapse in the superior thoracic sympathetic chain → postganglionic thoracic cardiac nerves to the cardiac plexus, OR
    2. Ascend the sympathetic chain to synapse in the cervical ganglia → postganglionic cervical cardiac nerves to the cardiac plexus

Cervical chain ganglia

GanglionLocationProjects to
SuperiorAdjacent to C2–C3Heart, head, and neck (hitchhikes on the carotid arteries)
MiddleAdjacent to C5–C6Heart and neck
InferiorAdjacent to C7; fuses with the 1st thoracic ganglion to form the stellate ganglionHeart, posterior cranial arteries, lower neck, and arm

Right/left distribution

  • Right-sided sympathetic fibers → right deep cardiac plexus → innervate the right heart and SA node
  • Left-sided sympathetic fibers → left deep cardiac plexus → innervate the left heart and AV node
Note: preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the heart come from T1–T5 — many textbook diagrams (and this one) forget to depict the T5 root, but it's part of the same pathway.

02. Autonomics: Sympathetic Effects on the CV System

Direct effects on the SA node, conduction system & myocardium

  • Increased heart rate (chronotropy)
  • Increased force of contraction (inotropy)
  • Increased impulse conduction (dromotropy)

→ all of these increase myocardial oxygen demand.

Direct effects on peripheral vasculature

  • Vasoconstriction
  • Increased blood pressure — the heart must work harder to push blood into tightened vasculature

Indirect effects on cardiac physiology

  • Decreased time for diastole (atrial filling) → decreased coronary blood flow → cardiac ischemia, and cardiac muscle death if severe enough
  • Counter-mechanism: direct sympathetic effects on the coronary vessels via β2-receptors cause relaxation/dilation, helping maintain myocardial blood flow during increased activity
  • Other effects: cardiac remodeling, impaired lymphatic drainage from the heart, and indirect effects from adrenal catecholamines

Effects of hypersympathetic activity

SideNode affectedResulting arrhythmias
RightSA nodeSupraventricular tachyarrhythmias — sinus tachycardia, paroxysmal SVT (PSVT)
LeftAV nodeEctopic foci → ventricular tachycardia (V-tach) and ventricular fibrillation (V-fib)
V-tach increases ventricular emptying inefficiency; V-fib markedly decreases the efficiency of ventricular contraction. Both ultimately decrease oxygen delivery to the body and worsen cardiac ischemia.
Practice Question

03. Autonomics: Parasympathetic Innervation & Effects

  • Parasympathetic innervation to the heart comes from the vagus nerve (CN X)
  • Can be affected by restrictions/somatic dysfunction of the OM (occipitomastoid) suture, OA, C1, C2, and the thoracic inlet
  • Right/left distribution mirrors the sympathetics: right vagus → right heart + SA node; left vagus → left heart + AV node

Effects of parasympathetic stimulation

  • Decreased heart rate (chronotropy)
  • Decreased force of contractility (inotropy)
  • Decreased impulse conduction (dromotropy)
  • Constriction of coronary arteries
  • Decreased blood pressure
  • Improved lymphatic drainage
In short: parasympathetic stimulation slows the heart down and gives it a chance to relax.

Effects of hyperparasympathetic activity

SideNode affectedResult
RightSA nodeSinus bradycardia
LeftAV nodeAV blocks
Practice Question

04. Chapman's Points for Cardiovascular & Renal Systems

There are two anterior and two posterior Chapman's points specific to the heart (myocardium). The adrenals and kidneys are also relevant to a cardiac workup — the anterior adrenal points are found just above the anterior kidney points, mirroring the actual anatomic relationship (adrenals sit on top of the kidneys).

05. Biomechanics: Cardiac Anatomy & Surfaces of the Heart

Three layers of the heart

  • Epicardium — visceral pericardium
  • Myocardium — cardiac muscle
  • Endocardium — endothelial cells lining the 4 chambers

Right side (right atrium/ventricle) collects deoxygenated blood and pumps it to the lungs; left side (left atrium/ventricle) collects oxygenated blood and pumps it to the body.

Surfaces of the heart

SurfaceDescription
BaseFlat, faces posteriorly; formed by the pulmonary veins entering the left atrium; level with T6–T9; associated with the pericardium, esophagus, and aorta
Sternocostal surfaceAssociated with the sternum and costal cartilages of the left 5 uppermost ribs
Diaphragmatic surfaceWhere the heart rests on the superior aspect of the central tendon of the diaphragm

External landmarks

Anterior landmarkPosterior levelAssociated with
Jugular notch, 1st ribT3Superior surface of the aortic arch
Sternal angle (manubriosternal joint)T5Insertion of the aorta into the heart
Xiphisternal jointT9Diaphragmatic surface of the heart, just superior to the epigastric fossa
Practice Question

06. Biomechanics: The Pericardium

  • Sac enclosing the heart, located between T4–T8
LayerDescription
Parietal — fibrous pericardiumStrong, dense collagenous tissue; blends with the tunica externa of the great vessels and the central tendon of the diaphragm, giving the heart stability
Parietal — serous pericardiumLines the inner surface of the fibrous pericardium
Pericardial spaceBetween parietal and visceral layers (analogous to the pleural space)
Visceral (epicardium)Serous layer that intimately follows the heart's contours; becomes contiguous with the parietal serous layer at the root of the heart (like the visceral/parietal pleura at the lung hilum)
  • Blood supply: pericardiophrenic vessels, plus branches from the bronchial and esophageal vessels
  • Innervation: visceral sensory fibers from the phrenic and vagus nerves, and the sympathetic trunks

07. Biomechanics: Pericardial Ligaments

The fibrous pericardium is anchored by several ligaments:

  • Bound to the central tendon of the diaphragm posteriorly and inferiorly (phreno-pericardial ligaments)
  • Bound to the sternum via sterno-pericardial ligaments anteriorly, with phrenic nerves embedded within
  • Adherent to the mediastinal pleura
  • Also includes vertebro-pericardial and xipho-pericardial ligaments
Clinical rationale: the pericardium and these ligaments can be strained by trauma (e.g., a seatbelt injury in an auto accident) or by pathology in the area — this is one reason cardiac cases benefit from a biomechanical/structural assessment, not just a purely medical one.

08. Biomechanics: SNS/PNS Structures & the Vagus Nerve

Key structures related to autonomic input to the heart — particularly the cervical spine, upper thoracic spine, and ribs. Visceral-somatic and somato-visceral reflexes to/from the heart occur at T1–T5, synapsing in the upper thoracic and/or cervical chain ganglia (superior adjacent to C2–C3, middle near C5–C6, inferior adjacent to C7).

The vagus nerve (CN X)

  • Originates in the medulla
  • Exits the skull via the jugular foramen (formed by the occipital and temporal bones), near the occipitomastoid suture
  • Has connections with the first two cervical somatic nerves (OA, C1, C2)
  • Enters the chest via the thoracic inlet, passing many fascial and bony structures along the way (lower cervicals, cervical fascia, upper thoracics, ribs, clavicles, Sibson's fascia, scapula, etc.)

09. Circulation: Coronary Arteries

ArterySupplies
Left coronary artery (LCA)Arises from the aorta; short, but distributes blood to a large area of myocardium — left ventricle, left atrium, Bundle of His, anterior interventricular septum
Left anterior descending (LAD)Anterior region of the left ventricle, down to the apex
Left circumflex (LCx)Posterolateral side of the left ventricle
Right coronary artery (RCA)Arises from the aorta; supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, SA node, and AV node
Posterior descending artery (PDA)Inferior wall, posterior interventricular septum, posteromedial papillary muscle
Right marginal artery (RMA)Runs along the anterior border of the heart
SA nodal arterySmall branch supplying the SA node
Practice Question

10. Circulation: Cardiac Veins

Veins largely run parallel to the arteries.

VeinDescription
Coronary sinusLargest vein draining the heart muscle; receives blood from the left ventricle, drains into the right atrium
Anterior right ventricular veinsGather from the right 2/3 of the right ventricle; end in the right atrium
Smallest/thebesian veinsDrain the right atrium and ventricle, emptying directly and individually into each chamber

11. Circulation: Lymphatic Drainage

DuctDrains
Right lymphatic ductRight side of the head, right upper extremity, right thoracic cage, right lung, and the entire myocardium
Thoracic duct (left)Pericardium, left lung, and the entire rest of the body
Note that the entire myocardium drains via the right lymphatic duct, regardless of which side of the heart is involved — relevant when thinking through lymphatic congestion in cardiac disease.

12. Screening: General Cardiac Evaluation

A thorough cardiac evaluation includes:

  • History and physical exam, including cardiac auscultation
  • Laboratory evaluation, including cardiac biomarkers/enzymes drawn serially to establish a trend
  • Electrical conduction studies: 12-lead ECG, ECG stress test
  • Structure/function imaging: chest X-ray, echocardiogram, stress echo, MRI/CT of the thorax (e.g., CT angiography), nuclear stress tests, PET scans
  • Internal cardiac evaluation: cardiac catheterization, angiography, coronary blood flow and pressure measurements
  • Vascular evaluation: Doppler ultrasound, MRI/CT of the vasculature
  • Kidney function (including vascular function): ultrasound with Doppler

13. Screening: Osteopathic Structural & Lymphatic Exam

On the osteopathic structural exam, evaluate how somatic dysfunction could affect autonomic tone, lymphatic flow, and biomechanics. Areas to evaluate:

  • OA, C1, C2
  • C3–C7
  • Upper thoracics
  • Clavicles
  • Upper ribs
  • Sternum
  • Diaphragm
  • Psoas

Also perform a Chapman's points screen, and remember to evaluate the cranial-sacral mechanism as well — think autonomics, lymphatics, and structure together.

Evaluating for lymphatic flow obstruction

Especially where edema is present, inspect and palpate:

  • Thoracic inlet
  • Abdominal diaphragm
  • Pelvic diaphragm
  • Axilla
  • Inguinal region & hip joint
  • Elbow
  • Knee (popliteal fossa)
  • Wrist
  • Ankle
At a minimum, always check the thoracic inlet and abdominal diaphragm for congestion or restriction of venous/lymphatic flow — remember, the diaphragm is one of the body's primary natural lymphatic pumps.
Practice Question

14. Screening: Treating the Whole Patient

  • Think like an osteopath — treat the person, not the disease. Consider body unity, including mind and spirit
  • Cardiac issues are frightening for patients and can create ripple effects across their whole life
  • Ask: how is this disease process affecting the patient's life and well-being? What's going on in this patient's life that could be affecting their health?
  • Consider: relationships, food, habits, medications, economics, and housing (or lack thereof)

15. Management: Myocardial Infarction

  • Address life-threatening issues first: oxygen, pharmaceuticals (aspirin through opiates for pain), and acute interventions as needed (e.g., cath lab)
  • Once stable, focus on optimal healing by decreasing O2 demand, heart rate, and arrhythmia propensity

Autonomics

  • Decrease facilitation in the upper thoracic and upper cervical spine
  • Vagus (parasympathetic): OM suture, OA, AA, C2 — techniques from a simple sub-occipital release to more specific approaches (MFR, HVLA, ME, BLT)
  • Sympathetics: address somatic dysfunction anywhere from T1–T5 (note the rotation direction — it matters later), plus the ribs (rib raising or specific techniques for specific dysfunctions)
  • Treat any Chapman's points found

Structure & function

  • Address elements influencing the work of breathing — to increase excursion, lymph flow, and venous drainage
  • C3–C5 (phrenic nerve to the diaphragm)
  • The diaphragm itself, and the thoracic cage (rib raising, HVLA, ME, BLT)

16. Management: Arrhythmias, Palpitations & Tachycardia

  • Medications, pacemakers, or defibrillators as necessary (e.g., for A-fib or V-fib)
  • Once stabilized, address the same autonomic areas as for MI:
    • Vagus: OM suture, OA, AA, C2
    • Sympathetics: T1–T5, ribs, and associated Chapman's points
  • Structure & function: C3–C5 (phrenic nerve to diaphragm), and the diaphragm itself (sub-occipital release, MFR, HVLA, ME, BLT; rib raising)

17. Management: Congestive Heart Failure

  • Medications and interventions as necessary
  • Autonomics: vagus (OM suture, OA, AA, C2); sympathetics (T1–T5, ribs)
  • Lymphatics: diaphragm, thoracic inlet; pumping/effleurage techniques for extremity edema — but these must be preceded by opening all pertinent lymphatic diaphragms
  • Structure: C3–C5 (phrenic nerve to diaphragm); the diaphragm itself, which is often flattened and overstretched from the heavy breathing required in CHF
  • Also address the pelvic diaphragm, and blockage points/baffles behind the knees, around the ankles, and in the soles of the feet
  • Lifestyle: avoid both overdoing and underdoing activity; decrease dietary salt; other dietary/lifestyle modifications as needed
Treating CHF reinforces the importance of balancing lymphatic flow with fluid overload — techniques like pumps and effleurage for pedal edema are only effective once the relevant lymphatic diaphragms have been opened first.
Practice Question

18. Management: Hypertension

  • Often requires multiple visits to develop the best regimen for each patient — this provides many opportunities to add consistent OMT supporting the body's own healing ability
  • Medications as necessary, including a blood pressure log
  • Autonomics:
    • Vagus: OM suture, OA, AA, C2
    • Sympathetics: T1–T5 (cardiac) and T10–T11 (renal)
    • Inferior mesenteric ganglion — supports optimal kidney and adrenal function
    • Chapman's points
  • Lifestyle: hydration with water rather than caffeinated drinks; a diet that decreases fat and sugar intake; mild-to-moderate exercise — even 5 minutes, multiple times a day, does real good
Remember to address both the cardiac AND renal systems in hypertension — the two are intimately linked autonomically (T1–T5 cardiac, T10–T11 renal, plus the inferior mesenteric ganglion for kidney/adrenal support).
As always: the most important person on the healthcare team is the patient.
Practice Question
